assessment.nobel_worthiness: The collateral-constraint mechanism in which credit limits and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks is a foundational idea in macro-finance. It underlies much of the post-2008 analysis of financial crises and is a standard tool in macroeconomics, corporate finance and policy modelling. The contribution is a clear theoretical insight with wide, practically useful application.
assessment.attribution: The central credit-cycles result is closely tied to Kiyotaki and Moore (1997). Gertler and Gilchrist are important extenders and empirical developers, but the core idea is cleanly attributable to the two proposed laureates. Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator work is related but partly overlaps with an earlier prize.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of confirmation, extension and use in quantitative macro and policy. The idea is fully mature, and the 2008 crisis added strong empirical relevance.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would also want to credit Gertler, given the three-laureate limit and the earlier recognition of the financial-accelerator line.
Relative standing against other macro-finance and New Keynesian contributions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and labour demand, together with the China-shock evidence on local labour-market adjustment to trade, changed how economists and policymakers understand inequality, automation and globalisation. The empirical design is transparent and the policy impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the trade-shock work, and Hanson is central to the trade-shock and regional-adjustment evidence. Dorn is an important co-author on the trade-shock papers. Katz and others (including the earlier task-model authors) contributed to the broader literature, so credit is somewhat diffuse.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from roughly 2003 to 2016 and have been widely replicated, extended and debated. The main empirical findings are well established, though the interpretation of long-run effects is still being refined.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the task framework and the trade-shock work as one prize-sized contribution or two.
Debate over long-run magnitudes and the identification strategy.
Attribution of the task framework to earlier authors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A systematic framework for analysing how political institutions, electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It integrates theory with cross-country and within-country evidence and has built a mature field.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the closest fit for the constitutional and electoral-rules programme and the associated book and papers. Besley is closely tied to accountability and state-capacity work. Acemoglu, Robinson and Johnson received a recent prize on institutions, so the incremental distinctiveness of this contribution must be weighed.
assessment.maturity: More than 30 years of development, with a large and well-confirmed body of work.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may reduce marginal appeal.
Identification is weaker in some of the cross-country evidence.
How strongly the committee weights theory-driven political economics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data are used to measure intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and policy impacts. This changed both the empirical standard and the policy conversation on opportunity. Methodological and substantive influence is very high.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear central figure, with Hendren and Friedman as the most closely tied collaborators. Katz is credited in the longlist through earlier Moving to Opportunity work. The collaborative, team-based nature of the research makes attribution to a few individuals less clean.
assessment.maturity: The central work is from about 2014 onward. The measurement results are widely replicated, but long-run causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects and policy follow-through are still being tested.
uncertainties: Relatively recent for a Nobel-level assessment.
Concerns about data access and replicability.
Whether the contribution is primarily measurement, or a lasting conceptual advance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshaped trade theory and empirics, introducing new channels for the gains from trade and the effects of liberalisation. The framework is a workhorse in international economics.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI and his broader role in new trade theory strengthen his case. Redding is a prominent developer, and Krugman's earlier prize partly overlaps with the subject area.
assessment.maturity: More than 20 years of confirmation and extension, with widespread use in empirical and quantitative trade work.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier new trade theory prize.
Competition from the quantitative trade models in B001 and from other trade candidates.
Whether Redding should be included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run tax-data series on top incomes and wealth reshaped the empirical and public debate on inequality, and offshore-wealth estimation opened a new area. The impact is large, though some of the contribution lies in measurement and synthesis rather than identification.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-incomes series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and tax havens. Atkinson, a key early figure, is deceased. Credit is shared across a large international network.
assessment.maturity: The top-incomes work has been established for two decades. The wealth-distribution and offshore estimates are more recent and contested.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth-inequality estimates and capital-return theories.
Mixed views on how much of the work is conceptual advance rather than measurement.
Politicisation of the topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of present bias, self-control problems and reference dependence brought psychologically grounded preferences into mainstream theory. They have applications in savings, pension design and consumer finance. The policy relevance is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Laibson (quasi-hyperbolic discounting and applications) and Rabin (psychology-informed theory, including reference dependence with Koszegi) are the leading theorists. O'Donoghue, Loewenstein and Koszegi are significant contributors. The 2002 and 2017 prizes already recognised behavioural economics, which complicates the marginal case and the selection among many credible contributors.
assessment.maturity: Several decades of development. The core models are widely used, although empirical support for some structural claims is mixed.
uncertainties: Prior behavioural prizes may reduce the appetite for another.
Credit among many contributors.
Replication and structural-identification debates around reference-dependent and present-bias parameters.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Legal origins and investor protection brought systematic cross-country evidence to the study of how law shapes financial development and corporate governance. The work is among the most cited in finance and law and economics, and it opened a large research agenda.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny, and the three proposed names are the most frequently combined with the legal-origins programme. Vishny is a fourth co-author on the foundational papers, which strains the three-laureate limit and complicates attribution. Shleifer has additional influential contributions in behavioural finance and corporate governance.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of use and critique. The qualitative finding that investor protection matters is well supported, but the legal-origins causal story is disputed.
uncertainties: Serious critiques of the legal-origins identification and of the coding of the legal-protection indices.
Four-person credit with a three-name cap.
Professional controversies surrounding one candidate.
